implementation_notes: ActiveSupport::Cache::Store#fetch is the pattern as a single call: it reads the key, invokes the block on a miss and writes the result with expires_in, so the read-check-populate protocol never appears in application code; delete or write is the invalidation step after the model write, and stores such as RedisCacheStore add race_condition_ttl to soften thundering-herd writes when a hot entry expires. The store is pluggable (MemoryStore, MemCacheStore, RedisCacheStore) and the same fetch call works across all of them, which is why Ruby has one dominant realization rather than several competing ones.
code_sketch:
class UserRepository
  def find(id)
    Rails.cache.fetch("user:#{id}", expires_in: 5.minutes) do
      User.find(id)                     # source of truth on a miss
    end
  end

  def update(id, attrs)
    User.where(id: id).update(attrs)    # store first
    Rails.cache.delete("user:#{id}")    # then invalidate
  end
end
pitfalls: fetch caches nil results by default, so a missing record is remembered as absent and stops hitting the database - pass skip_nil: true or handle negative caching deliberately.
With RedisCacheStore no expiry is set by default and eviction depends on the server's maxmemory policy; set expires_in on every fetch instead of relying on the store.
RedisCacheStore is fail-safe: when Redis is unavailable, fetches are all misses and writes are dropped, so the application keeps working but a silently absent cache tier must be monitored.
Cached Ruby objects are serialized (Marshal/MessagePack): deserializing cache payloads is a trust boundary, and key shapes and versions must change across deploys that alter the data.
